Name: narration_subspace_suppression
Title: Think in Shorthand: Separating a Narration Subspace from Computation to Suppress Performative Reasoning
Short Hypothesis: Reasoning models carry two largely separable residual-stream subspaces: a computation subspace that carries out and updates the latent answer, and a narration subspace that governs verbose, human-facing presentation of already-computed results. Overthinking is over-activation of the narration subspace after computation is effectively done. Suppressing the narration subspace (while leaving the computation subspace intact) makes the model 'think in shorthand,' cutting tokens with minimal accuracy loss, and does so more precisely than a single verbosity/length direction.
Related Work: Recent work establishes that CoT is often performative or unfaithful and that latent answers form early: Reasoning Theater (2026) probes performative CoT and early-exits; TTS / 'Can Aha Moments Be Fake?' (2025) labels steps decorative vs load-bearing and finds a single steerable TrueThinking direction; State over Tokens (2025) reframes tokens as externalized state; Causal Bypass / CMI (2026) shows answers can be causally independent of CoT text. Efficiency-steering work (Manifold Steering, CREST, ThinkEdit, ASC) steers along a single verbosity/length direction. All prior work either (a) treats decorative-vs-genuine as a per-step binary, (b) reads a single latent 'answer' or 'verbosity' direction, or (c) reactively early-exits. None hypothesizes or tests a *dimensional decomposition* of the residual stream into a computation subspace that must be preserved and a separable narration/presentation subspace that can be suppressed. Our contribution is (1) constructing and causally validating these two subspaces via contrastive activation collection (terse vs verbose renderings of identical computations) plus disentanglement, (2) showing overthinking corresponds to sustained narration-subspace activation after computation completes, and (3) a training-free intervention that projects out the narration subspace during generation, which is finer-grained than a single length direction because it preserves the orthogonal computation subspace by construction.
Abstract: Reasoning language models routinely 'overthink,' generating verbose chains of thought long after they have effectively solved a problem. Prior interpretability work explains this as performative or decorative reasoning and either labels individual steps or steers a single verbosity direction. We propose a sharper, dimensional account: the residual stream contains two largely separable subspaces—a computation subspace that performs and updates the latent answer, and a narration subspace that governs verbose, human-facing presentation of results already computed. We hypothesize that overthinking is sustained narration-subspace activation after computation is complete, and that suppressing the narration subspace while preserving the orthogonal computation subspace lets the model 'think in shorthand' with minimal accuracy loss. We construct the two subspaces via contrastive activation collection—prompting models to render identical computations tersely versus verbosely—followed by difference-of-means and orthogonalization to isolate a narration direction set that is, by construction, orthogonal to the components that carry the latent answer. Across GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, and GPQA on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we verify the subspaces are separable by testing that suppressing narration does not degrade a latent-answer probe while suppressing computation does. We show narration-subspace activation stays high during overthinking after residual work (via truncate-and-resume) reaches zero. Finally, we introduce a training-free generation-time projection that removes the narration subspace and compare token savings at equal accuracy against verbosity steering, TTS-style pruning, and reactive early-exit. Our work reframes overthinking as an over-narration mode and offers a precise, interpretable efficiency mechanism.
Experiments: 1) Subspace construction: Collect contrastive activation pairs by prompting the model to produce a TERSE and a VERBOSE rendering of the *same* underlying computation (e.g., same worked solution, one written as a compact derivation, one with narration/verification/asides), across a held-out set of problems. Compute difference-of-means activation vectors per layer to get candidate narration directions; do the same across easy (more performative) vs hard (more genuine) problems as an alternative narration signal. Assemble a low-rank narration subspace via SVD of the difference vectors. 2) Separability test (core validation): Train a linear latent-answer probe (predicting eventual final answer) as the computation readout. (a) Project out the narration subspace from activations and re-measure latent-answer probe accuracy—hypothesis: minimal drop. (b) Project out a matched-rank random subspace and an actual computation subspace (from the answer probe weights)—hypothesis: computation-subspace removal sharply drops probe accuracy while narration removal does not. Report probe AUROC/accuracy under each ablation; quantify orthogonality (principal angles) between narration and computation subspaces. 3) Overthinking dynamics: Segment CoT into steps; at each step read narration-subspace activation magnitude. Measure residual work via truncate-and-resume (accuracy after forcing termination at step t). Hypothesis: narration-subspace activation stays elevated after residual work hits zero, and its post-completion integral predicts wasted tokens (tokens after last accuracy-changing step) better than trace length, absolute verbosity-direction projection, and a confidence probe (compare regression R^2). 4) Causal intervention (training-free): During generation, subtract the projection onto the narration subspace from residual activations at selected layers (fixed coefficient sweep). Evaluate on GSM8K, MATH500, AIME, GPQA. Baselines: no intervention, single verbosity/length steering (ASC/Manifold-style), TTS-style post-hoc step pruning, Reasoning-Theater-style probe early-exit, fixed truncation. Metrics: accuracy, mean tokens, token-reduction-at-equal-accuracy, wall-clock speedup. Key comparison: does narration-subspace projection Pareto-dominate the single-direction verbosity baseline (finer preservation of computation)? 5) Qualitative check: inspect generations under narration suppression to confirm the model retains derivation steps but drops decorative narration/verification asides; human/LLM-judge rating of correctness-preserving compression. 6) Failure/underthinking analysis: on hard items where narration overlaps with genuine verification, measure accuracy drop vs suppression strength and identify a safe operating point. 7) Generalization: transfer the narration subspace across datasets and model scales without recomputation.
Risk Factors and Limitations: The clean separation of narration and computation subspaces may not hold—verification/narration can carry genuine computation, so suppressing narration might harm accuracy on hard problems (this trade-off is measured directly and a near-null result on separability is itself informative). Contrastive terse/verbose prompting may not elicit representations that match spontaneous overthinking, biasing the narration direction; we mitigate with an alternative easy-vs-hard difference signal and cross-validate. Latent-answer probes are reliable mainly for extractable answers, so we restrict to math/multiple-choice. The narration subspace may partially coincide with the single verbosity direction, in which case the dimensional framing yields little gain over prior steering (though the separability analysis remains a contribution). Projection at generation time can push activations off-distribution and introduce errors; coefficient sweeps and validity checks address this. Results may be model-family and scale specific.
